question_text: Why is Zn²⁺ diamagnetic whereas Mn²⁺ is paramagnetic?

mark_split.label: Zn²⁺ configuration and why it is diamagnetic
Mn²⁺ configuration and why it is paramagnetic

verification.note: Unit 11 (d and f Block Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 8 ("8. d & f BLOCK ELEMENTS"), book pp.91-94, which prints this question on book p.91 as VSAQ 1. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK NOTATION: the printed question writes the charges as Zn+2 and Mn+2; the standard form Zn²⁺ and Mn²⁺ is used here. The printed answer is correct as far as it goes. ADDED HERE: the spin-only moments are computed, μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, giving 0 BM for Zn²⁺ (n = 0) and √35 = 5.92 BM for Mn²⁺ (n = 5); and the trend is stated with its exception — Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) are the two diamagnetic, colourless ions at the ends of the first transition series while every ion between them is paramagnetic and coloured.

steps.label: Zn²⁺ is diamagnetic
lines: The two 4s electrons are removed first,
All ten d electrons are paired, so the
With no unpaired electron, Zn²⁺ is
steps.why: The 4s electrons leave first when a d-block atom is ionised, so the ion is written 3d^x 4s⁰ and not 3d^(x-2) 4s². Zn²⁺ then has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ set in which every orbital holds a pair, so n = 0 and the spin-only moment is zero. Zn²⁺ is one of the two ends of the first transition series where this happens; the other is Sc³⁺, which is 3d⁰. Both are diamagnetic and colourless, while every ion between them is paramagnetic and coloured.
common_mistakes: Writing Zn²⁺ as [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². The 4s electrons are removed first, so the ion is 3d¹⁰ 4s⁰.
Calling a filled d¹⁰ set paramagnetic. Paramagnetism needs at least one unpaired electron, and d¹⁰ has none.
steps.memory_tip: Count unpaired electrons, not total electrons. d¹⁰ gives zero and d⁵ gives five.
steps.margin_note: Write the configuration of the ION, not the atom. The configuration plus the words "no unpaired electrons" earns this mark.

steps.label: Mn²⁺ is paramagnetic
lines: By Hund's rule the five d electrons
occupy five orbitals singly, so n = 5.
With five unpaired electrons, Mn²⁺ is
steps.why: Hund's rule fills the five d orbitals one electron at a time before any pairing begins, so 3d⁵ is the half-filled set with five unpaired electrons — the largest number available in the first transition series. That is why Mn²⁺ has the largest spin-only moment of the series, 5.92 BM, and why Zn²⁺ at the other extreme has none.
common_mistakes: Pairing the five d electrons into two orbitals. Hund's rule fills all five orbitals singly first.
Giving the moment as 5 BM. The formula is √(n(n+2)), so five unpaired electrons give √35 = 5.92 BM.
steps.memory_tip: d¹⁰ is fully paired and gives 0 BM; d⁵ is half filled and gives the largest value, 5.92 BM.
steps.margin_note: The word paramagnetic must sit next to "five unpaired electrons". The number 5.92 BM is extra credit, not the mark.

insider_note: Both marks are configuration marks. Write the ION configuration with 4s⁰ shown, then the unpaired-electron count, then the word diamagnetic or paramagnetic. The magnetic moment is not asked for here, so add it only after both halves are written.
